# The Witness Who Did Not Graduate {#sec-3-07}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — Hoover, War, and the Archive State · 1919–1939
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** What does the pipeline look like from outside it?

**The answer.** It looks like a place you can walk out of. Steinbeck spent six
years at Stanford, accumulated ninety-three units, never took a degree, and left
in 1925 without an intention of returning. What he did instead — work alongside
the migrants and ranch hands the credential exists to sort him away from — became
the counter-archive: the record of the people the institution's records do not
count.

**The mechanism.** Elite network reproduction, observed by its refusal. This
chapter tests the previous one. If Stanford in the 1920s was a credentialing
interface between private money and public authority, then the interesting
question is what happens to someone who declines the credential. The answer is
that he loses the network and keeps the material, and the material turns out to be
worth a Nobel Prize.

**The key fact.** Ninety-three units. Six years. No degree. He enrolled to satisfy
his parents, chiefly his mother, and took only the courses that interested him —
which is to say he used the university as a library rather than as a ladder.

**The human anchor.** Steinbeck, in the one-room shack behind a larger house in
Palo Alto where he lived in his final year, walking distance from the tower Hoover
would raise over the campus.

**Excluded voices.** This is the chapter where they speak, and that is the point.
The bindlestiffs, the Filipino and Mexican field crews, the Dust Bowl migrants of
the late thirties. Act III's other chapters describe the class that manages
crises. This one describes the class that absorbs them, through the eyes of the
only man in the act who chose to stand in it.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the institution's power lies in sorting rather
than teaching by showing that the same campus, in the same decade, produced both
the archive of world power and its most durable indictment — and only credentialed
one of them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Opens with the number: ninety-three units over six years, and no degree. It is
the most eloquent transcript in this book.

Steinbeck arrived at Stanford in 1919, the year Hoover's War Collection was
founded. He enrolled because his parents wanted it, principally his mother, and he
treated the catalogue as a menu — English, classical literature, and, in a detail
that shapes everything he later wrote, marine biology and ecology. He never
declared himself a candidate for anything. He left repeatedly, worked as a ranch
hand and a farm labourer, came back, left again. In his final year he lived in a
one-room shack behind a larger house in Palo Alto. In 1925 he left for New York
and did not come back, and never built a relationship with the university
afterwards.

The chapter sets this against what the same campus was doing in the same years.
Hoover was assembling in Palo Alto the largest private collection of documents on
war and revolution in the world — the archive of how power moves. Under Jordan's
long shadow the university had lent its scientific authority to a programme of
sterilisation under the 1909 law. And the Graduate School of Business, founded in
1925, was formalising the credential as an instrument.

One institution, one decade, three outputs: an archive of power, a science of
exclusion, and a young man walking out the gate to go and live among the excluded.

The argument is not that Steinbeck was Stanford's opposite. It is that he was
Stanford's product in the way that matters least to Stanford and most to the
record. What he took from the place was ecology — the habit of reading a system by
looking at what it consumes — and he applied it to labour. *In Dubious Battle*,
*Of Mice and Men*, and *The Grapes of Wrath* are what happens when the
university's analytical method is turned on the university's economy.

Closes on the asymmetry of the two archives. Hoover's is a building with his name
on it, at the centre of the campus, visible from the freeway. Steinbeck's is a
shelf of novels, and the campus he left has a plaque.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
What does the pipeline look like from outside it?
:::

Ninety-three units. Six years. No degree.

That is John Steinbeck's Stanford transcript, and it is the most eloquent
document in this book. He enrolled in 1919, attended intermittently until 1925,
reached the standing of a junior, and left for New York without a diploma and
without any intention of returning. He never established a relationship with the
university afterwards.

He had arrived the same year Herbert Hoover's collectors were buying leaflets in
Europe for the archive described two chapters ago. Two men, one campus, one
decade, two records of the twentieth century — and only one of them was
credentialled.

## Why he was there at all

He was there because his parents wanted it, principally his mother, who was a
schoolteacher and who expected her son to acquire the qualification that a young
man of his background was supposed to acquire.

He treated the catalogue as a menu. He took English and classical literature. He
took courses in marine biology and in what would now be called ecology, and that
selection turns out to matter more to what he later wrote than anything else in
the transcript. He did not declare himself a candidate for a degree and did not
organise his coursework toward one.

This is a person using a university as a library, which is a coherent thing to
do and is not what the institution is for. The institution's product is the
credential. A student who takes the teaching and declines the certificate has
consumed the part that costs the university money and refused the part that
generates its position.

## The leaving

He left repeatedly and came back. In between he worked.

He was a ranch hand. He worked on road crews and in a sugar-beet operation. He
did manual labour alongside migrant workers and the itinerant single men the
period called bindlestiffs — men who carried their bedding and followed the
harvests, who had no fixed address, no property, and no standing.

In his last year at Stanford he lived in a one-room shack behind a larger house
in Palo Alto, a few minutes' walk from a campus where his contemporaries were
being fitted for the positions described in the previous chapter.

In 1925 he left for New York, worked as a labourer on the construction of
Madison Square Garden and briefly as a newspaper reporter, failed to establish
himself, and came back to California to keep writing.

## The other campus

Set this against what the same institution was doing in the same years.

Hoover's War Collection was being assembled — the documentary record of how
power had moved through Europe, purchased with American dollars in collapsed
currencies and shipped to Palo Alto. Under Jordan's long influence the
university had supplied intellectual authority to a sterilisation programme that
was, by the 1920s, operating at a scale unmatched in any other state. The
Graduate School of Business opened in 1925 to formalise the management
credential.

One institution, one decade, three products: an archive of power, a science of
who counts, and a certificate of fitness to manage.

And a young man walking out of the gate to go and live among the people the
third product was designed to distinguish him from.

## What ecology gave him

The chapter's argument is not that Steinbeck was Stanford's opposite. It is that
he took from the place the one thing it taught him that it did not intend as a
credential, and then applied it to the wrong subject.

Ecology reads a system by looking at what it consumes. It asks what the inputs
are, where the energy goes, which populations expand, which are depleted, and
what happens at the margins when conditions change. It is not interested in the
intentions of the organisms.

Steinbeck learned that framework in a laboratory and then spent his career
applying it to human labour. His later collaboration with the marine biologist
Ed Ricketts made the method explicit — *The Log from the Sea of Cortez* is
substantially an argument about non-teleological thinking, about looking at what
is rather than at what ought to be — but the habit is visible long before that.

*In Dubious Battle*, in 1936, is a novel about a strike in the California fruit
country written with a clinical detachment that satisfied neither the growers
nor the organisers. *Of Mice and Men*, in 1937, is about two of the itinerant
ranch workers he had worked beside. *The Grapes of Wrath*, in 1939, follows a
dispossessed farming family into the California agricultural labour system and
documents what that system does to the people it draws in.

That is what happens when the university's analytical method is turned on the
university's economy. The same intellectual move that produces a research
programme in marine biology produces, applied to a farm, a description of an
extractive system with a workforce it consumes and discards.

The reception was appropriate to the argument. *The Grapes of Wrath* was banned
and burned in Kern County. The Associated Farmers organised against it.
Steinbeck was accused of exaggeration, of propaganda, and of communism, and he
was followed by people who wished him harm. He was also read by everyone.

## The counter-archive

Here is what the two archives contain.

Hoover's holds what institutions produced: decrees, proclamations, official
correspondence, the printed output of parties and governments. It documents
power from the inside, which is what makes it valuable and what determines its
shape.

Steinbeck's is a shelf of novels, and it holds what institutions did not record:
what it was like to be in the labour force that Act II chapter 11 described
being recruited, used, and blamed in a hundred-year sequence of nationalities.
By the 1930s that workforce was substantially made up of white American migrants
from the Dust Bowl states, which is a large part of why this particular round
produced a national literature. The Chinese workers of the 1870s, the Japanese
farmers dispossessed by the Alien Land Law, and the Filipino crews of the 1920s
had no comparable chronicler with access to a national publisher.

That is not a criticism of Steinbeck. It is the archive problem from Act I
chapter 1, still operating: the record reflects who had the means to make one.

## The report he was asked to write

There is one document that makes the comparison between the two archives exact,
and it is not a novel.

In 1936 the *San Francisco News* commissioned Steinbeck to write a series of
articles on the migrant labour camps in the Central Valley. He travelled with
Tom Collins, who managed a federal resettlement camp at Arvin, and the pieces
ran as "The Harvest Gypsies" in October of that year.

They are reporting rather than fiction, and they are specific in exactly the way
the Voice Guide of this project asks for. They give the number of people in a
squatter camp, the condition of the water, the arithmetic of a family's income
against the cost of food, the piece rates paid for each crop, and the mechanism
by which growers' associations coordinated wages downward before a harvest. They
name the vigilante organisations and describe how they operated.

This is an administrative record of a labour system, compiled from the inside,
by someone who had done the work. It is the same kind of document as a mission
register or a Commission for Relief ledger, except that it was produced by
somebody with no institutional interest in the outcome, which is why it counts
different things.

The articles were reprinted as a pamphlet by a Bay Area committee and are
substantially the factual foundation of *The Grapes of Wrath* three years later.
Steinbeck also worked from Collins's own camp reports, and dedicated the novel
in part to him.

The mechanism is the same one this act has been describing throughout. Somebody
went and looked, wrote down what was there, and the writing became the record.
The difference is who was counted.

## The asymmetry

Hoover's archive is a building. It is two hundred and eighty-five feet tall, it
carries his name, it stands at the centre of the campus, and it is visible from
the freeway.

Steinbeck's is a shelf. The campus he left has a plaque and a collection in the
library, and his name is on a centre at a state university forty miles south —
San José, not Stanford.

Both are records of the same California in the same decades. One was endowed.

He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962. Phil Knight received his MBA
from the Stanford Graduate School of Business the same year.
